newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.S., Britain unable to get UN vote on Iraq yet.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Britain unable to get UN vote on Iraq yet.

text.p: The United States and Britain failed on Friday to obtain a Security Council vote banning Iraqi officials from travelling abroad without permission until Baghdad cooperates with U.N. arms inspectors.

Britain's ambassador Sir John Weston said envoys from both countries were going to consult privately with other members, presumably, China, Russia, France and Egypt who have reservations on the draft resolution.
Russia has already submitted a rival resolution that condemns Iraq for barring the inspectors from three sensitive sites but makes no reference to any tightening of sanctions.

Its ambassador Sergei Lavrov, who is also the current Council president, said no meeting had been scheduled. "I am not instructed to say anything and I am not even authorised to think in my capacity as president," he quipped.

In Denver, U.S. and British envoys at the Group of Seven summit of industrial nations sought to drum up support for the resolution with French and Russian leaders, who along with the United States, Britain and China are permanent members of the 15-seat council.
A resolution has to be adopted by nine votes and no veto from a permanent member.

The new measures would ban travel by members of the Iraqi army, police and intelligence services as well as the civiiian defence and military industrial commission unless authorised by the council's sanctions committee. They also would suspend a regular council review on stringent trade sanctions imposed on Iraq until Baghdad cooperates.

Iraq has been under sanctions since its troops invaded Kuwait in August 1990. One condition for lifting sanctions on oil exports is to scrap its weapons of mass destruction and related documents. The council maintained U.N. inspectors are to have free access to suspected sites.

Over the past year the council has been split on strong action against Iraq, with the United States losing ground among members of the original coalition that drove Iraqi troops from Kuwait in 1991. The $1.3 billion in arrears owed to the United Nations have further eroded Washington's clout.

The council last Friday issued a relatively mild statement deploring a series of incidents in which U.N. inspectors said Iraqis had endangered U.N. helicopters and their crews assisting U.N. ground teams. Since then inspectors have been turned away from three sites they attempted to visit.
Chief U.N. arms inspector Rolf Ekeus said this week Iraq was in "clear violation of council resolutions."

"If Iraq is allowed now to decide what we should inspect, when we should inspect it, I think the value of the whole mechanism set up after the Gulf War would be put into question," he said, referring to the U.N. special commission (UNSCOM) in charge of scrapping dangerous Iraqi armaments.

Ekeus, who will leave UNSCOM on July 1 and will be succeeded by Australian U.N. envoy Richard Butler, speculated it "may be because we are changing leadership that Iraq is now trying to change the ground rules somewhat."

Iraqi Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz, in a letter to the council, said access to some sites had been denied recently because of concern the inspections were not to carry out UNSCOM's mandate but to "detect the arrangements made for the security of Iraq, its leadership and the personnel involved."

Aziz said the UNSCOM team was allowed to inspect 40 out of the 43 sites to which it sought access. Denial of access to the other sites "cannot be interpreted as a decision by the government of Iraq to prevent the special commission implementing its mandate, as Mr Ekeus alleges," he added.
